A_target.statement:
Let $f$ be [[Definition:Continuous Real Function|continuous]] on $\closedint a b$ and let:
:$\displaystyle \map F x = \int_a^x \map f t \rd t$
Then $F$ is [[Definition:Differentiable Real Function|differentiable]] on $\openint a b$ with $\map {F'} x = \map f x$.

B_source.statement:
Let $f$ be continuous on $\closedint c d$.
Then there exists $\xi \in \closedint c d$ such that:
:$\displaystyle \int_c^d \map f t \rd t = \map f \xi \paren {d - c}$

substitutions.the interval [c, d]: the small interval between x and x + h

object_map.reformulation: Express the difference quotient of the integral as a value of f at an intermediate point.

validity_conditions: Continuity of f is needed both for the mean value theorem and to pass to the limit.
Additivity of the integral over subintervals is used to isolate the increment.
proof_plan:
For $x \in \openint a b$ and small $h \ne 0$, by additivity of the integral:
:$\displaystyle \map F {x + h} - \map F x = \int_x^{x + h} \map f t \rd t$

By the [[Mean Value Theorem for Integrals]], there is $\xi_h$ between $x$ and $x + h$ with:
:$\displaystyle \int_x^{x + h} \map f t \rd t = \map f {\xi_h} h$

Hence:
:$\dfrac {\map F {x + h} - \map F x} h = \map f {\xi_h}$
